title: Which way is up?
hook: Today almost every map puts north at the top. What did a medieval mapmaker put there?

knows: that maps have north at the top
roughly where Europe, Asia and Africa are
doesNotKnow: that north-up is a convention that has changed
how medieval European world maps were laid out

misconception: North has always been up because that is the natural way to draw the world.
objective: The learner can explain that which direction is at the top of a map is a choice, and that medieval European world maps such as the Hereford map put east at the top.

claims.text: The Hereford world map (Hereford Mappa Mundi) dates from about 1300.
claims.source: Hereford Cathedral, 'The Mappa Mundi' (usually dated c. 1300). From memory, not checked online. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Hereford Mappa Mundi dated c. 1300 (web search: Wikipedia and Hereford Cathedral summaries give about 1300, installation c. 1290 or later).

claims.text: The Hereford map puts Asia at the top, Europe at lower left and Africa at lower right.
claims.source: The map follows the T-O scheme: Asia fills the upper half, Europe the lower left quarter, Africa the lower right quarter (Hereford Cathedral; British Library 'T-O maps'). From memory, not checked online. Note: on the original, the labels for Europe and Africa are famously swapped; the layout of the land is as stated. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Search results (Wikipedia 'Hereford Mappa Mundi'): Asia fills the top, Europe the lower left quarter, Africa the lower right quarter; the continent labels for Europe and Africa are swapped on the original, as the source note says. Consistent with east at top (north then points left, south right).

claims.text: The Hereford map, like other medieval European world maps, has east at the top.
claims.source: Hereford Cathedral; Harvey, Mappa Mundi: The Hereford World Map (1996). From memory, not checked online. The lesson also derives it: turning the globe so the layout in c2 holds puts east at the top (topDirection(90) in Demo.tsx). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Hereford has east at the top (Wikipedia; Hereford Cathedral). 'Like other medieval European world maps' is accepted as 'many/typical' (T-O mappae mundi are east-oriented; this is where 'orient' comes from) - it is not claimed for all; wording note: 'many' is safer than an implied 'all'. Stage derives east-at-top from the projection.

claims.text: The Hereford map is centred on Jerusalem.
claims.source: Hereford Cathedral, 'The Mappa Mundi'. From memory, not checked online. Used for the stage caption and the globe's centre. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Jerusalem is the centre of the Hereford map (Wikipedia; Hereford Cathedral). Stage centre 35.2E 31.8N matches Jerusalem.

claims.text: The word orient comes from the Latin for rising, the east, where the Sun rises.
claims.source: Oxford English Dictionary, 'orient': from Latin oriens, oriens -entis 'rising, sunrise, east', present participle of oriri 'to rise'. From memory, not checked online. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Latin oriens, orientis 'rising, east', present participle of oriri 'to rise' (OED; Lewis and Short). | v2 (2026-10-14): question no longer gives the layout; reveal now follows two turns the learner made; previous verification void, needs re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Web search 2026-10-14: Etymonline and Merriam-Webster: Latin oriens 'rising, the east', present participle of oriri 'to rise'. Stage wording 'Orient is Latin for rising' is a loose but acceptable gloss.

claims.text: Al-Idrisi drew his world map in 1154 with south at the top.
claims.source: The Tabula Rogeriana, made for Roger II of Sicily in 1154, is oriented with south at the top (Bodleian Library, MS. Pococke 375 copy). From memory, not checked online. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Tabula Rogeriana, completed 1154 for Roger II, is oriented south-up (Wikipedia 'Tabula Rogeriana'; Dickinson College and map-dealer descriptions). Surviving copies are later but the map was drawn in 1154. | v2 (2026-10-14): question no longer gives the layout; reveal now follows two turns the learner made; previous verification void, needs re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 19): Web search 2026-10-14: Wikipedia 'Tabula Rogeriana' and map-dealer descriptions: completed 1154 by al-Idrisi for Roger II, south at the top. Matches the reveal.

claims.text: North at the top is today's convention for almost every map.
claims.source: Hook and reveal. A statement about modern practice (national survey sheets, atlases, web maps all print north up by default). No source checked; needs one or softening. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Searches (UCSB Geography 'Why is North Up on Maps', GeoGarage, Flowing Data) agree north-up is a convention that was settled in Europe by the early 1500s and is the default for modern maps. 'Almost every' is a general statement about default practice; some maps are deliberately oriented otherwise (track-up navigation, local wayfinding). Non-blocking.

claims.text: The Earth has no top, so which way is up on a map is a choice.
claims.source: A sphere has no preferred direction in space for a picture of it; the stage turns one orthographic view (d3-geo geoOrthographic, third rotation angle) and every turn is equally correct. The lesson makes no claim about why north-up won. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Logical: a sphere has no preferred up in a picture of it; the stage turns one orthographic view in 90 deg steps and each is equally correct.

recall.question: Why is north at the top of most maps today?
options: The North Pole is the top of the Earth
It is a convention; medieval European maps put east at the top
Compasses only work with north up
recall.why: A ball has no top. Which way is up on a map is a choice, and it has changed: the Hereford map put east up, al-Idrisi put south up.
